before.html: On February 21, 2026, Malaysia's trade ministry said Malaysia had signed its Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the United States but had not ratified it (given it final legal approval). The ministry said Malaysia was assessing recent U.S. legal and policy developments. The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. The statement reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This setting, with replacement tariffs, differs from the comparison used here: ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [35].

On October 22, 2025, Malaysia's trade minister said of Lynas: "We will not stop them from exporting to markets of their choice," naming South Korea, Japan and the United States. Malaysia separately has a moratorium on exporting unprocessed rare earths. Lynas said in May it was engaged with customers in Japan, the United States and Europe. The sources reviewed identify no restriction under consideration for this supply. Sources: [45], [43].

after.html: Section 301, a separate U.S. trade law, allows tariffs after findings and procedures when a country denies agreement rights or fails to enforce commitments concerning labor and the environment. In October 2025 the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), the U.S. trade agency, proposed duties on Nicaragua partly over labor abuses. These duties were not yet imposed. Sources: [38], [39], [40].
